title: QSTAR: Quantum Selective Transfer with Adaptive Routing
authors: Saim Rehman, Nouhaila Innan, Muhammad Shafique
abstract: Quantum transfer learning (QTL) is often evaluated by replacing a classical classifier with a fixed variational quantum head, but this hides a key question: when is the quantum branch actually useful? We propose QSTAR: Quantum Selective Transfer with Adaptive Routing, a selective QTL framework that keeps high-confidence classical predictions and routes only low-confidence samples to a fallback branch. Using a frozen ResNet18 backbone on Fashion-MNIST, we compare manually designed QTL heads, KetGPT-designed quantum heads, and parameter-matched classical baselines under a common data split and optimization schedule. Standard QTL heads reach at most 57.0% accuracy, while the strongest KetGPT head in the main filtered sweep reaches 78.5% accuracy and 0.785 F1-score. Although the strongest fixed classical head remains higher at 81.6%, selective routing gives the quantum branch a clearer role. On low-confidence samples, KetGPT #180 improves accuracy over a parameter-matched MLP fallback by 6.82, 4.31, and 3.03 percentage points at thresholds of 0.70, 0.80, and 0.90. At the full-system level, Adaptive KetGPT-QTL reaches 80.9% accuracy and 0.807 F1-score, outperforming the adaptive classical baseline. A separate compact-circuit ablation identifies KetGPT #160 as a stronger fixed-head candidate, reaching 81.9% accuracy with only 10 quantum parameters and 9 gates. These results suggest that architecture-searched quantum heads are most useful as targeted fallback branches for uncertain inputs rather than uniform replacements for classical classifiers.
summary: This paper introduces QSTAR, a selective framework for Quantum Transfer Learning that routes samples to a quantum circuit head only if the initial classical prediction is low-confidence. The results demonstrate that this targeted approach significantly boosts accuracy by leveraging quantum computation where it is most needed, suggesting quantum heads are best used as specialized fallback tools rather than general replacements.
main_problem: The evaluation of Quantum Transfer Learning (QTL) often incorrectly assumes the quantum head replaces the classical classifier, obscuring when the quantum component is genuinely useful.
main_result: Selective routing, which only passes low-confidence samples to a quantum fallback branch, significantly improves performance over standard QTL methods and outperforms adaptive classical baselines.
method: The authors propose QSTAR, a selective framework that uses sample confidence scores ($	au$) to route inputs: high-confidence data stays with the classical prediction, while uncertain data is passed to a parameterized quantum circuit head.
model_or_system: The model utilizes a frozen ResNet18 backbone for feature extraction on Fashion-MNIST. The classification involves comparing linear classical heads, MLP fallbacks, and various architecture-searched quantum circuits (KetGPT-designed heads).
key_observables: Accuracy ($	ext{Acc.}$), F1-score, and the performance improvement of the quantum branch specifically on low-confidence samples.
important_parameters: The confidence threshold $	au$ used for adaptive routing; circuit parameters (e.g., 10 parameters, 9 gates) in ablation studies.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the utility of quantum heads is conditional on input uncertainty rather than being a universal replacement for classical methods.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the QSTAR methodology. Table I compares fixed-head transfer learning results, and Table II shows adaptive routing performance across different confidence thresholds ($	au$).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the limitation of standard QTL evaluation, proposes the selective QSTAR framework using adaptive routing based on sample confidence, presents quantitative comparisons against various baselines (classical/quantum heads), and concludes by arguing for the role of quantum circuits as targeted fallback mechanisms.
why_interesting: While focused on machine learning, the concept of selectively engaging complex physical models (like quantum circuits) only when classical methods fail or are uncertain mirrors concepts in open quantum systems where specific environmental coupling or measurement protocols are only applied under certain conditions.
